scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Warlord's Dream: Kōwakamai
This is Kōwakamai. 15th–17th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Founded by Momonoi Naoaki (Kōwakamaru) in the 15th century, the art evolved from 14th-century kusemai.
It was supported by warlords like Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu before falling into obscurity by the 19th century.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically used for warrior-class entertainment, it often features sorrowful tales of defeat and loss.
It is currently performed annually on January 20 at Tenman-jinja.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performances involve three players: a principal tayū and two supporting actors (waki and shite).
They wear suwō tops and long hakama, do not wear masks, and do not impersonate characters, focusing instead on rhythmic narration.
on_screen: Formation: Three players standing in a group.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music consists of oral recitation of ballads.
Instrumental melodic arrangements have been restored by the Kōwakamai Preservation Society.
The music is defined by the rhythmic oral recitation of dramatic prose, focusing on the vocal delivery of sorrowful narratives.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Atsumori — Kōwakamai Preservation Society
scenes.music: the music brief's underscore at its own tempo; drop narration under the hook of a verified recording if licensed, else original

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear a suwō top and a long version of the hakama trouser.
They wear different types of eboshi hats.
Performances are held at shrines, such as the Tenman-jinja in Ōe.
on_screen: Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Momonoi Naoaki (founder), Yamamoto Shirozaemon (founder of the Daigashira School), and Ōsawa Jisuke Yukitsugu.
The primary surviving variant is the Ōe Kōwakamai, preserved in the Ōe district of Miyama, Fukuoka.
The Kōwaka family branches (Hachirokurō, Yajirō, and Kohachirō) and the Daigashira School.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Kōwakamai is parent of kusemai: Kōwakamai is believed to have evolved from this 14th-century dance form.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Performances are held as part of a local festival at the Tenman-jinja shrine; outsiders should respect the ritual nature of these shrine-based events.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: Discover the medieval Japanese dance that turned battlefield sorrow into a haunting, rhythmic art form.
